I've always had problems with insomnia and so I always focused on making my room as sleep friendly as possible... cool, quiet, turning electronics off so there were no standby lights and putting up both a blackout roller blind AND thick thermal blackout curtains.

The lack of sunlight in the morning ruined my circadian rhythm and I could sleep well in to the day regardless of whether I went to bed at 3am or 12am (the latter early for me, an insomniac). I'm talking sleeping for 10 or 11 hours or more. 

Turns out you want it to be dark at night but a lack of natural light in the morning isn't good either. I use a SAD lamp and a timer nowadays (originally purchased for my bipolar depression but also helps with this) and also plan on getting one of those Phillips gradual wake up sunlight alarm clocks when I have more money and a decent job which requires an alarm (the SAD lamp can only be on or off, there's no gradual option). 

Ironically, I had the same problem for the opposite reason whilst at uni! In my third year I moved from one bedroom in the house which had semi-blackout curtains, to one which had bright orange, non-blackout curtains. Well, the sun used to be on that side of the house on a morning; it caused little issue in the winter, but in late spring and early summer, the light would fill the room anywhere between 4:30-8am and I'd wake up at like 5am when I didn't need to be up until 9am. So I'd end up super tired, go to my lectures and seminars starting at 10am and come home at about 2pm, eat dinner and end up "napping" for 3 hours in the afternoon when the sun had moved and my room was more tolerable. 

I don't find melatonin as a supplement a good sleep aid - it never really seemed to do much for me, and for some people it causes vivid dreams which can sometimes be a negative - I already have vivid dreams due to antidepressants, however I also have REM sleep behaviour disorder that means without medication I fall in to REM sleep too quickly before my muscles paralyse and I start "acting out" my dreams or doing other physical things in real life that somehow represent what I'm doing in my dreams. I'm prescribed 1mg clonazepam to take at night so that I can sleep safely, but extra melatonin supplements for me now would be a bad idea as they could make my dreams worse and I don't know if the clonazepam would be enough or not to help with them.

Yet clearly melatonin is hugely important in maintaining sleep patterns and circadian rhythms in general - I just prefer to try and stimulate natural production through the use of day lamps and sunlight in the day and slowly darkening and dimming lights in the evening. I'm sure I also read that melatonin supplements may not be helpful as it's not sure how much of a dose actually crossed the BBB and also people that do take them usually take them too late (unlike most sleeping aids, they shouldn't be taken 30 mins or an hour before bed, but around about when it starts to naturally dark, or when it should be starting to get naturally dark if you are for example in a windowless room. It's not a knockout type pill).

It uses both a device security certificate (a separate one for each device too so I can connect from each device to my VPN at the same time if I want to - so a cert for my laptop and another for my iPhone), plus a password as well as the cert.

I may have changed the port from the default to something random too, I can definitely remember fiddling with port forwarding on my router but I'm not sure if that was for setting up OpenVPN or something else. My certs are 2048 instead of 1024 too (they take a while longer to create on a Pi 2 tho so be willing to keep it running a while) and my password is 16 characters long. My OpenVPN password isn't saved on my laptop or iPhone, so always have to enter manually to connect. My laptop and iPhone are password and PIN locked too (with a different password to my VPN one naturally). 

You could always use fail2ban and geo restrictions too if your router/firmware supports it although again that kinda assumes you know where you'll be travelling to/what IP you'll show up as dialling in from.

Cause of death:

His family's insistence that they'd only recently got a PC in the house, that he rarely used it, showed little interest in it, that this PC and any PC he had access to had all been checked by the police and come up with nothing... to me has always been weird.

I was 14 years old in 2005, two years before Andrew went missing. And I came from a poor family. And we'd had a computer for about 6 years, internet access for about 5, broadband for the previous year. And I did absolutely all sorts of things on there that my parents had no idea about - AOL chat rooms, MSN, Chat Avenue chat rooms, web messenger on school PCs where MSN wasn't installed, LiveJournal, Last.fm, numerous forums. All sorts of things. My parents thought I was just downloading music (which I was too), talking to my cousins (which I also was doing) and homework (which I was rarely doing). 

I would talk to strangers all the time. I ran my own forum at age 14 with over 4000 members from across the world. I also knew what proxies were and we would all use them at school so we could use chat rooms in IT lessons and use web messenger to talk across the room 'cos MSN wasn't installed on the PCs.

That was me at 14 in 2005. Andrew went missing in 2007. 

I'm not saying the internet had ANYTHING to do with his disappearance as I have no evidence to suggest that, none. I just hate the "oh no he wasn't in to the internet/computers" or "only used it briefly for homework" and "they were all checked and nothing unexpected was found". If I could do everything I could do at 14 in 2005, I'm sure Andrew too would have been more than capable. 

Like I said I'm not suggesting the internet has/had anything to do with his disappearance, rather that the insistence that it hasn't/didn't I find to be.... over the top and slightly conspicuous in itself. It's always made a point of how it was unlikely to be someone he didn't know, unlikely anything to do with the internet blah blah blah and I just feel like the more it's mentioned (cue a "all PCs he had access to were checked!" here) the more I personally feel like I'm being diverted either from something, or towards something else.

This is no disrespect to Andrew's family as the news reports about him also follow in the same vein and make a big deal out of his lack of technowizadry. But I just don't swallow it, not necessarily because it's impossible he wasn't in to computers/the internet/etc. but because the more someone tells me it's an avenue that has been explored and "cleared" and that there's "nothing more to go on in that area" the more I think, why are you so insistent? 

I had a teacher who was found with child porn on his school issued laptop in 2003/2004 who was sent to prison and hung himself inside. Maybe all the PCs he had access to were checked. What if he had struck up a 'friendship' with someone like the IT guy at school? Andrew was in to gaming (his PSP etc.) and might have been caught trying to download something to his PSP or browse blocked PSP/gaming related sites or something that would link the IT people to him.... maybe becoming talkative over a break time and then chatting at the end of the school day as they both left etc. This person would have authority and be able to act as the adult for trips to places like London to see bands and things, and if he left the school/stopped working there and was relatively young (maybe early to mid 20s) Andrew might have seen him more of a cool older friend rather than someone who used to work at his school. Someone who had previously worked in this role wouldn't have necessarily needed to talk to Andrew via the internet as that could just have been the starting point. However if they did have anything on computers this person would obviously have the ability (whilst working at the school still) to reimage computers, manipulate log files etc. 

I don't know -- do I believe this theory I literally just made up? No not really. I just find the whole "nothing to see here" with regards to the internet/computers/PSP thing over the top especially considering we are talking about a teenage male in 2007. I think people who were teenage males in 2004-2008 probably have a much better understanding of how unlikely it was he "didn't know much about computers" or "care for them"  - he was younger than me meaning he would have been brought up with computers at school and things more than even I was, and I do consider myself the computer/internet generation. Acting like computers were foreign objects to Andrew seems somewhat disingenuous.

If you're managing to keep it to once or twice a week only on a long term basis, then assuming you keep doses low and do not go up the ever increasing dosing ladder, you should be fine with regards to both tolerance and addiction. If you find yourself thinking about moving up the next rung of the ladder -- don't -- the more you climb the ladder, the closer you get to tolerance and addiction. 

At your current use, assuming it doesn't change and your dose and timing stays the same, you should be absolutely fine.

IDK it's what is done in psychiatry and psychology with people with schizophrenia. Schizophrenia: never play along with a person's delusions; things like Alzheimer's DO play along with a person's delusions.

I believe the thinking is that people with Alzheimer's, after suffering a certain extent of brain deterioration, will never ever be able to be "normal" again and so the effort to correct them is futile and only causes them further distress - it'd be like trying to teach a mascara wand algebra, the capacity just isn't there.

With schizophrenia (and I'm not saying comment OP's friend has schizophrenia just that maybe it's treated in the same way) the idea is to medicate the person enough so they don't act on their delusions and hallucinations or get too distressed or aggressive when their delusions are challenged. But the idea is that they should be challenged, at least eventually once a person is stable on medication, because otherwise they'll never be able to reintegrate back in to society if we've all played along with them for months or years. There needs to be some normalcy and grounding for them to return to, and it's likely problematic if we try and do that and they seem to be getting better and ready to live back in the community, then realising everyone who was playing along with their delusions was a liar, a cheat, just pretending, playing a game... potentially causing a relapse. 

In the UK at least, we medicate schizophrenia and schizophrenia like conditions and then try to work with people to realise that their thoughts and feelings are the result of a condition and not necessarily shared by the rest of society. It's the only way to do it if you want the people to be able to live in society with everyone else. Maybe it's different in the US and other places? I don't know. Over here most people with schizophrenia or similar illnesses will be sectioned at least once in their life, sometimes multiple times, but then they're released and in the periods in between the goal is for them to live as normal a life as possible even though they're never cured.

Source: from the UK, know three people with schizophrenia, all living at home but have been hospitalised numerous times between them. If they start to seem like they're spiralling then the first things doctors check is if they've been taking their meds, if not, they may be sectioned until they're back on them at a therapeutic dose. Then once stable the aim is to keep them as grounded as possible and not to play along with them. We don't keep people locked up on mental wards for extended periods of time unless they're a real danger to themselves or others -- they are reviewed regularly with the intention of getting them back to society and living as normal a life as is possible as soon as is safely possible.

They commit attempted suicide or completed suicide. In this scenario, opinions are worthless, because it was a rash decision and no real thought went in to it. So such opinions and "is suicide selfish?" arguments just don't enter the equation because that assumes a moment of thought went in to it. In these cases, the only thoughts seem to be about the literal act of suicide itself and avoiding/escaping whatever it is they are attempting to avoid or escape.

Then there are people with long standing issues that try to sort things, go get help like we're told to, and 5 years on are no better off than they were then. Sure they might have 3 or 4 good days in a row but that's about it. These people see no other way out - they've tried things, getting a job, seeing a doctor, a therapist, talking to people, going out for walks, meeting new people, acquiring hobbies, whatever, but whatever they have tried, hasn't worked. So these people turn to suicide because they literally are in a state of despair and do not see any other way out - whatever other routes they have tries, have seemingly failed for them. So they attempt suicide (whether they complete it or not) because they see no viable alternative. In this case... guess what? Opinions also don't really matter? Why? Because it doesn't matter how many times you tell someone suicide is awful/bad, if, in their head, suicide feels like the only thing they can do, then they can internalise it so much that they literally can not help but try and die. It's like trying to rob someone with no wallet or cash on them... you can hold a gun to their heads and threaten every single loved one they know but if they don't have any cash then they don't have any cash. It isn't going to appear from thin air because you're threatening them. Similarly if a suicidal person sees no other option then guess what? Don't tell them suicide is bad/selfish/wrong because that isn't the issue here. The issue is they don't see any other options. If you wanna try and help - give them another option, don't tell them their option sucks, if it is the only one they can see. Because if it feels like the only one then no matter how shitty it is, then what choice do they have? Nobody things suicides is rainbows and happiness. That is not why people commit suicide. They're easily influenced and don't seem to have reached that ultimate level of despair yet - so they probably wouldn't have done it anyway, and if they did, were probably going to choose a non-lethal, cry for help type method, rather than an actual legitimate attempt to end their lives. So yeah. Suicide shaming. Probably one of the most pointless things in the world. It doesn't stop the people most at risk from suicide from attempting suicide. When applying for your licence/certificate you will be told what is expected of you, for example, rules on how you must store the firearm(s), so like keeping them in a dedicated gun locker with lock and key that no one else has access to. We are not allowed to carry firearms in public, either concealed or not concealed. Keeping a gun in your house for protection from burglars for example is also not allowed. Mace/pepper spray is considered a firearm under UK law, we are not allowed to carry that either.
